entry.title: Introduction to Balances
entry.content:
In a complex world of business and finance, understanding a company’s financial standing is paramount for all stakeholders: management, investors, creditors, and employees. While various reports offer pieces of the puzzle, two statements stand out as fundamentals in financial reporting: the balance sheet and the cash flow statement. These documents provide essential and complementary insights, and offer a dual lens through which to examine a company’s financial health, stability, and operational efficiency.

Assets represent what the company owns, from tangible items like cash, inventory, and property, plant, and equipment, to intangible assets such as patents or goodwill. Liabilities represent what the company owes to others, including short-term obligations like accounts payable and expenses, and long-term debts like loans and bonds. Equity represents the residual interest in the assets of an entity after deducting liabilities: the owners’ stake in an organization.

The cash flow statement offers detail as to where an organization’s money comes from, and where the money goes after it has been received. These two reports provide interrelated pieces of information: the balance sheet is what the organization owns and owes, while the cash flow statement is how those assets were obtained and the disbursement of debts and equity.

Exchange of Assets and Liabilities

Double-entry accounting requires that every transaction effects at least two accounts. Transactions involving cash-for-product or cash-for-service, from the perspective of a business, typically effect cash (temporary liability) and inventory (asset) accounts.1 As cash is received by a business, it is taken on as a liability until a product is delivered or a service is rendered. Once the product or service delivery process occurs, the revenue is switched from a liability to an asset.2 For all intents and purposes, the liability of cash is exchanged for the asset of inventory or human capital and labor.

The transaction’s money, products, and services are temporarily held in “escrow accounts”. As the customer receives their product(s) or service(s), the escrow account is depleted until no outstanding balances remain. Retailers may appear to gloss over this process when transactions occur through cash registers, however the process is always observed similar to the more stringent remote transactions. Because direct exchanges at a retail counter are more immediate, the process is so fast it happens quicker than may be perceived. The process allows for recognition of very short-term, as well as longer-term, liabilities:3 the seller’s acceptance/receipt of payment until the buyer’s acceptance/receipt of the good or service.4 Most retailers view the process as instantaneous wherein physical ownership is governed by a cash register.

Once the cash is recorded as a liability in an “escrow” account, there are additional entries whose purpose is to decrease liability cash along with corresponding increases in asset cash.1 This process occurs in the retail industry by looking at the unit price and the quantity receivedaccepted by the customer, and then appropriately transitioning the amount of funds from unearned to earned revenue. Similarly, there is the replication of processes for the “escrow accounts” of products and services before receipt by the customer. These product and service accounts maintain what is owed to customers: cash, products, and services.

  1. Cash is traditionally viewed as an asset in accounting. The accounting systems for many businesses use an “escrow account” for handling unearned revenue. That is, the money received is a liability until all obligations have been fulfilled, e.g. going from unearned to earned revenue. ↩ ↩2

  2. Revenue is unearned when cash is provided without immediate and commensurate delivery of product or service. Unearned revenues occur in a variety of businesses where cash is accepted prior to delivery of products or services: subscription services, property rental, online retail, insurance, etc. ↩

  3. The liability can exist for nanoseconds as the appropriate transactions are recorded, or may be months or years. The technique temporarily creates an outstanding commitment, effectively setting aside a portion of received monies, to prevent overspending and ensure funds are available in the case the obligation cannot be fulfilled. ↩

  4. It is possible a buyer gets cold feet once the initial payment has been made to the seller. If the buyer never receives the goods they paid for, it is incumbent upon the seller to return/refund the initial payment. There may be laws which require the repayment within a certain amount of time if the goods or services cannot be procured or rendered. ↩
